newsitem.title: UK: New Labour no worry for British derivatives market.
newsitem.headline: New Labour no worry for British derivatives market.

text.p: The prospect of Labour sweeping to power in the next British election so far has failed to send investors scurrying to the derivatives market to hedge against the outcome.

A decline in the speculative use of derivatives in the wake of scandals such as Barings, coupled with the Labour Party's attempts to assuage its "tax and spend" image are expected to mean less frenzy in the markets.

"The usual pre-election rise in volatility is manifesting itself later than usual," said a broker at a major British brokerage in London. "This time the market is much happier with the prospects of a Labour victory."

The broker noted that the implied volatility of short sterling options rose to more than 50 percent before the last election. It is currently trading around 10 percent -- even though the election, which could toss out the Conservative party which has held power since 1979, must be held by May.
Analysts said recent statements from Labour's economics spokesman underlined the market-friendly approach opposition leader Tony Blair has adopted.

Earlier in the week, Labour's Gordon Brown pledged that public spending would not be increased beyond the levels already planned by the Conservative Party for the first two years in office. He also said tax rates would not be raised.

"This time around there is much less uncertainty now Gordon Brown has made tax commitments," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW in London. "There are deep divisions in the Conservative Party and the lack of sensible debate over Europe is something the City would like to put behind it."

The Conservative Party's wrangling over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) has been regarded as one of the reasons for the relative underperformance of British debt assets, compared with European counterparts in Spain and Italy.
Adams said the volatility of gilts and short sterling would start a muted rise in the next few months, as the economy appeared to be heating up, and a rate rise was unlikely ahead of the election.
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at the Cooperative bank in London said Labour's lead in the polls was so much greater than in 1992 that there won't be such a startling rise in volatility.
"There's also a genuine argument about whether a Labour government is a positive or a negative for the market," he said.
And Britain's national election appears rather less important to international investors than the question of whether Britain will be part of EMU or not.
"That's the real issue," said Beauchamp. "A Labour victory could be good for gilts purely because they are very pro-Europe."

A broker on the floor of London's International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) said another issue which has decreased volatility is the decline in the speculative use of options and futures. In the wake of some well-publicised debacles which gave derivatives a bad name, people are a lot more cautious about using them, the broker said.
According to data from LIFFE, in 1996 short sterling options volume fell 34 percent from the previous year, while gilt options dipped 22 percent.
That continued the slide from 1995, which saw short sterling options volume decline almost 17.5 percent from 1994, while gilt options volume was down 25 percent.
In contrast, volume in Italian BTP options has grown 138 percent in the same two-year period.

However, volume is expected to improve in April, when the gilt options which expire close to the expected May date of the election start trading. June gilt options expire May 22. -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6137
